body_md: B-tree updates pages in place so reads stay fast but random writes pay seek cost. LSM buffers writes in memory then flushes sorted runs so ingest screams while reads check several levels.
code:
// writes: memtable insert O(1), reads merge levels
// pick LSM for ingest, B-tree for range scans
hook: LSM loves writes, B-tree loves reads.
output:
write: memtable insert O(1); read: merge mem + levels
// ingest screams (LSM); range scans stay local (B-tree)

quiz.explain: LSM batches writes sequentially while B-tree keeps sorted pages for reads.
options: LSM for write throughput and B-tree for read locality
quiz.q: When do you pick LSM over B-tree?

takeaway: Choose LSM for write bursts and B-tree for range reads.
trap: Using B-tree for 100k writes per second without batching.

body_md: WAL appends every mutation to sequential log before applying it. On crash you replay the log so committed data survives even if memtables and pages never flushed.
hook: WAL first, applause after crash recovery.
output:
entry fsynced in WAL, then in memtable
// crash -> replay WAL; no committed write lost

quiz.explain: Append-then-apply plus replay gives durability without random writes.
options: Append to WAL then apply and replay on crash
quiz.q: What order makes writes durable?

takeaway: Append to the log first then replay it after a crash.
trap: Applying to memory before the log is durable.

body_md: SSTables are immutable sorted files flushed from memtables. They store keys with block indexes and checksums so reads binary search blocks and compactions merge them without locking writers.
hook: Immutable sorted files that make reads mergeable.

quiz.explain: Immutability lets readers snapshot files while mergers rewrite them.
options: Immutable sorted runs with indexes for lock-free reads
quiz.q: Why are SSTables immutable?

takeaway: Freeze sorted runs so reads and merges never block writes.
trap: Updating SSTables in place and breaking snapshots.

body_md: Bloom filters are bit arrays that answer maybe-present fast. Size them by expected keys and target false positive rate, then skip SSTables whose filter says definitely-not-present.
code:
if !filter.may_contain(&key) { continue; } // skip sstable
// else open block index
hook: Skip disk reads with a maybe-no filter.
output:
filter says no -> SSTable skipped, zero I/O
// says maybe -> open block index (tuned false positives)

quiz.explain: Bloom says no with certainty and yes with tuned false positives.
options: Cheap negative lookups before disk reads
quiz.q: What do Bloom filters guarantee?

takeaway: Use Bloom filters to skip SSTables that cannot hold a key.
trap: Treating a maybe-yes as proof the key exists.

body_md: Compaction merges SSTables and drops tombstones. Leveled compaction bounds read levels with more write work while tiered compaction batches merges with cheaper writes and slower reads.
hook: Leveled reads fast, tiered writes cheap.

quiz.explain: Leveling rewrites more but keeps fewer overlapping runs per key.
options: Leveled for read latency and tiered for write throughput
quiz.q: Leveled versus tiered compaction tradeoff?

takeaway: Pick leveled compaction for reads and tiered for ingest speed.
trap: Running no compaction until disk fills with tombstones.

body_md: Postgres B-tree indexes serve equality and ordered ranges with logarithmic seeks. Index low-cardinality flags alone and the planner skips them, so pair with selective columns or partial indexes.
code:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_ts ON orders(user_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1;
hook: B-tree wins when the filter is selective.
output:
Index Scan using idx_orders_user_ts (user_id = $1)
// selective leading column prunes pages

quiz.explain: Composite leading columns prune pages for selective predicates.
options: Composite B-tree on selective leading column
quiz.q: Best B-tree for user timeline queries?

takeaway: Index selective leading columns and keep ranges ordered.
trap: Indexing a boolean alone and expecting faster scans.

body_md: GIN indexes map tokens to row lists so full text and array containment avoid full scans. They cost slower writes and bigger size, so use them for search tags and JSONB containment.
code:
CREATE INDEX idx_docs_tsv ON docs USING GIN(to_tsvector('english', body));
SELECT * FROM docs WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ plainto_tsquery($1);
hook: GIN turns text search into index lookups.
output:
Bitmap Index Scan on idx_docs_tsv
// token -> row-list lookup; no full scan

quiz.explain: GIN posts token to row mapping for containment queries.
options: GIN for full text and array containment
quiz.q: When is GIN the right Postgres index?

takeaway: Use GIN for text search and array containment workloads.
trap: Putting GIN on a hot counter column with constant writes.

body_md: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows actual rows versus estimates plus buffers and timing. Look for seq scans on big tables, nested loops exploding, and wrong row estimates needing ANALYZE or better stats.
code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
hook: Stop guessing plans, measure actual rows.
output:
Index Scan ... actual rows=20 vs estimate; Buffers: shared hit
// fix stats/plan gaps before adding indexes

quiz.explain: Actual versus planned rows reveal bad stats and wrong join choices.
options: Compare actual rows and buffers against the plan
quiz.q: What do you read in EXPLAIN ANALYZE first?

takeaway: Compare actual rows with estimates before adding any index.
trap: Adding indexes without checking buffers and actual timing.

body_md: Pool size follows cores and latency, not wishful thinking. Little math says concurrent slots near core count times one plus wait over service time, then cap per Postgres host around a few hundred.
code:
-- pool ~= cores * (1 + wait/service)
-- 8 cores, 20ms wait, 5ms query -> ~40 conns
hook: Pool math beats pool mythology every time.
output:
8 cores * (1 + 20/5) = ~40 conns
// cap per host in the low hundreds

quiz.explain: Too many connections thrash context switches and memory.
options: Size pools from cores and latency then cap per host
quiz.q: How do you size a Postgres pool?

takeaway: Size pools from cores and latency then enforce a hard cap.
trap: Opening thousands of direct connections per service.

body_md: Read replicas replay the primary log so heavy writes create lag. Serve stale-tolerant feeds from replicas and read-your-write paths from primary or wait for replay position.
code:
-- route critical read to primary
-- SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(); -- check lag
hook: Replicas lag exactly when you need them most.
output:
primary read: fresh; pg_last_wal_replay_lsn shows lag
// stale-tolerant -> replica; read-your-write -> primary

quiz.explain: Lag spikes under write bursts break read-your-write assumptions.
options: Stale reads from replicas and critical reads from primary
quiz.q: How do you survive replica lag?

takeaway: Send tolerant reads to replicas and critical reads to primary.
trap: Reading own write from a lagging replica.

body_md: Partitioning splits one table by key for pruning while sharding spreads data across hosts for scale. Partition first for time ranges, shard when one node cannot hold writes or connections.
code:
CREATE TABLE events_2026_10 PARTITION OF events
FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-10-01') TO ('2026-11-01');
hook: Partition to prune, shard to survive growth.
output:
CREATE TABLE // events_2026_10 holds Oct 2026 only
// inserts route by date; scans prune to the partition

quiz.explain: Partitions prune locally while shards add independent capacity.
options: Partition for pruning on one node and shard for multi-node scale
quiz.q: Partitioning versus sharding rule?

takeaway: Partition single tables for pruning and shard clusters for capacity.
trap: Sharding before exhausting indexes and partitioning.

body_md: Hash each node to many points on a ring and walk clockwise to place keys. Adding a node steals only neighbor ranges, and virtual nodes even out hot spots from uneven hashes.
code:
let idx = ring.iter().find(|v| v.hash >= h)
    .unwrap_or(&ring[0]).node; // clockwise owner
hook: Walk the ring clockwise to find your data.
output:
h -> first vnode with hash >= h (wrap to ring[0])
// new node steals only neighbor ranges

quiz.explain: Virtual nodes spread load so one join moves little data.
options: Ring with virtual nodes for minimal remapping
quiz.q: Why use consistent hashing with virtual nodes?

takeaway: Map nodes to ring points so joins move only neighbor ranges.
trap: Using plain modulo and reshuffling all keys on resize.

body_md: Quorums trade latency for safety with W plus R above N. Write to W replicas and read from R so the sets overlap and the reader always sees the latest acknowledged write.
code:
// N=3, W=2, R=2 -> overlap guarantees latest read
if w_ok >= 2 && r_overlap { return newest; }
hook: Overlap your quorums or lose your writes.
output:
N=3, W=2, R=2: sets overlap -> newest write returned
// strong reads while a quorum is reachable

quiz.explain: Overlap forces every read set to include a fresh replica.
options: Keep W plus R above N so read and write sets overlap
quiz.q: What makes quorum reads see latest writes?

takeaway: Keep write plus read counts above replica count for overlap.
trap: Setting W plus R below N and claiming strong reads.

body_md: Vector clocks attach per-node counters to each write so replicas compare histories. Concurrent counters mean conflict to merge while dominated counters mean one version safely wins.
code:
// a:[2,1] vs b:[2,2] -> b dominates a
// a:[2,1] vs c:[1,2] -> concurrent, merge needed
hook: Counters that detect sibling writes honestly.
output:
[2,1] vs [2,2]: b dominates a -> b wins
[2,1] vs [1,2]: concurrent -> merge needed

quiz.explain: Dominated histories resolve silently while concurrent ones merge.
options: Per-node counters to separate causal from concurrent writes
quiz.q: What do vector clocks capture?

takeaway: Track per-node counters to tell causal order from true conflicts.
trap: Using wall clock timestamps to order concurrent writes.

body_md: PN-counter CRDT keeps one grow-only counter per replica for increments and one for decrements. Merge takes max per slot and value equals increments minus decrements, so replicas converge without coordination.
code:
struct Pn { inc: Vec<u64>, dec: Vec<u64> }
fn value(&self) -> i64 { self.inc.sum() - self.dec.sum() }
hook: Counters that merge without ever arguing.
output:
value = sum(inc) - sum(dec), merged by per-slot max
// offline increments converge; no lock

quiz.explain: Per-replica grow-only slots merge by max and stay correct.
options: Per-replica increment and decrement vectors merged by max
quiz.q: How does a PN-counter stay correct offline?

takeaway: Split counters per replica and merge slots by maximum value.
trap: Sharing one integer across replicas with concurrent writes.

body_md: Kafka exactly-once uses idempotent producers plus transactions across partitions. Wrap consume-transform-produce in one transaction so retries never duplicate downstream effects.
hook: Exactly once is a transaction, not a hope.
output:
offsets + outputs commit in one transaction; retries dedupe
// needs broker: init -> begin -> send_offsets -> commit

quiz.explain: Transactional offsets plus idempotence make retries safe.
options: Idempotent producer with transactional consume and produce
quiz.q: What gives Kafka exactly-once pipelines?

takeaway: Combine idempotent producers with transactions spanning offsets and output.
trap: Committing offsets before downstream writes succeed.

body_md: CDC streams row changes from the WAL with Debezium into Kafka so caches and search stay fresh. Use outbox table plus connector to publish atomically with the local transaction.
code:
-- INSERT INTO outbox(event, payload) in same txn
// debezium tails wal -> kafka topic -> consumers
hook: Turn Postgres WAL into live event streams.
output:
row lands in outbox in-txn; debezium tails WAL -> kafka
// caches/search consume exactly the commits

quiz.explain: Outbox plus log tailing publishes only committed rows.
options: Outbox table with WAL connector for atomic publish
quiz.q: Reliable way to publish Postgres changes?

takeaway: Publish changes through an outbox table tailed from the log.
trap: Writing to DB and Kafka as separate unguarded steps.

body_md: Redis eviction picks victims when memory fills. Use noeviction for billing writes, allkeys-lru for caches, volatile-ttl for sessions, and set maxmemory plus sampling to bound latency.
hook: Pick victims before memory picks your outage.
output:
maxmemory 2gb; over limit -> LRU victim evicted
// volatile-* only evicts keys with expire; billing uses noeviction

quiz.explain: Caches tolerate LRU loss while critical writes must error loudly.
options: Match eviction policy to data criticality and TTLs
quiz.q: How do you choose a Redis eviction policy?

takeaway: Match eviction policy to data value and expiry pattern.
trap: Using allkeys-lru on data you cannot afford to lose.

body_md: Cache stampede hits when hot key expires and thousand threads recompute. Add jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate, and background refresh so only one worker rebuilds the value.
hook: One expiry should not thundering-herd your DB.

quiz.explain: Staggering expiry plus async refresh avoids synchronized misses.
options: Jitter TTLs with stale serve and single refresh
quiz.q: How do you stop a cache stampede?

takeaway: Jitter expiries and serve stale data during background refresh.
trap: Expiring all hot keys on the same second.

body_md: Singleflight dedupes concurrent loads for one key so ten requests share one future. Wrap the fallible fetch in the call and clones receive the same result without hammering Postgres.
hook: Ten requests in, one query out.
output:
one db.load_user(42); all 10 waiters get the same v
// errors are NOT cached as values

quiz.explain: Shared in-flight future collapses duplicate work safely.
options: Share one in-flight fetch across duplicate concurrent keys
quiz.q: What does singleflight do in Rust?

takeaway: Collapse duplicate concurrent loads into one shared future.
trap: Caching errors from singleflight as if they were values.

body_md: Postgres MVCC keeps old row versions so long transactions bloat tables. Tune autovacuum, index HOT-friendly updates, and monitor dead tuples before sequential scans slow down.
code:
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_all_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10;
hook: Dead tuples are silent latency debt.

quiz.explain: Vacuum reclaims dead versions and refreshes planner stats.
options: Vacuum aggressively and watch dead tuple counts
quiz.q: How do you control MVCC bloat?

takeaway: Vacuum early and track dead tuples before scans suffer.
trap: Holding day-long transactions on a hot write table.
